extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in social criticism, political philosophy, and cultural commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards for judging social, political, and domestic proposals (e.g., property, family, revolution) as argued in a cultural/political essay. Focuses on whether ideas are restorative, rooted in history, practicable, and sensitive to class context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowness of the new ideas / limiting effect of the future
rubrics_metrics.description: “The modern prophetic idealism is narrow because it has undergone a persistent process of elimination. We must ask for new things because we are not allowed to ask for old things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals that celebrate futurity for whether they are narrow because they avoid revisiting or attempting older ideals; check for a fear-of-the-past motive. The essay argues modern enthusiasm for the future often masks avoidance of difficult past ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of restoration — claim the freedom to restore
rubrics_metrics.description: “A clock, being a piece of human construction, can be restored by the human finger to any figure or hour. In the same way society, being a piece of human construction, can be reconstructed upon any plan that has ever existed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing solutions, include restoration of past institutions/plans as legitimate options rather than assuming past forms are impossible. The writer explicitly claims the right to propose older social arrangements if they solve present evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine futurity is rooted in the past (historical test for innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the men in history who have really done anything with the future have had their eyes fixed upon the past.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge claims of originality by checking whether they draw on or recover past models (e.g., Renaissance artists dug up antiquities). Historical precedence can be evidence of substantive originality rather than mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check future-oriented rhetoric for ignoring past precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern writers often predict future ideals while ignoring that similar ideals existed in the past (e.g., advocates of European unity ignoring Roman/medieval precedents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical test: when reading advocacy for a future ideal (peace, social democracy, etc.), check whether the authors acknowledge relevant historical precedents and past attempts; omission is a warning-sign of superficiality or amnesia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'untried' ideals from disproved ones (lost causes may have merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a thing has been defeated it has been disproved. Logically, the case is quite clearly the other way. The lost causes are exactly those which might have saved the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat suppressed or failed movements as disproven systems; assess whether they failed because they were not fully lived/tried. Examples: Catholic Church ideal and French Revolutionary ideals are described as unfulfilled rather than refuted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property as democratic art / limited creation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “Property is merely the art of the democracy. It means that every man should have something that he can shape in his own image... the special joy of man is limited creation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate property not only as wealth but as the vehicle for individual self-expression within limits; value placed on small, delimitable ownership (garden, house) that allows personal creativity and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of wealth negates true property (enemies of property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large capitalists who absorb others' land are described as enemies of property because they destroy the limitations that make property meaningful: “They do not want their own land; but other people’s.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess property systems for whether they preserve distinct, limited holdings that allow personal shaping; critique systems where aggregation erases boundaries and thus the democratic/artistic function of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family/home as primary anarchic institution beyond easy state control
rubrics_metrics.description: “The home ... is older than law, and stands outside the State... the State has no tool delicate enough to deracinate the rooted habits and tangled affections of the family.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing reforms affecting family life, account for the practical limits of legal/state intervention; the essay treats family relations as intimate, delicate, and often resistant to legal solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage and other durable bonds justified by surviving the 'breaking point'
rubrics_metrics.description: “In everything worth having... there is a point of pain or tedium that must be survived... The success of the marriage comes after the failure of the honeymoon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate marriage (and similar commitments) by whether they create structures that help people endure the inevitable early difficulties; commitment/coercion can be reframed as encouragement to reach lasting rewards rather than mere oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domesticity is not inherently dull — context matters (the wildness of domesticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the moderately poor the home is the only place of liberty and anarchy: “For the plain, hard-working man the home is not the one tame place in the world of adventure. It is the one wild place in the world of rules and set tasks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware assessments of domestic boringness that arise from the viewpoint of the wealthy; evaluate domestic life with regard to socioeconomic position — for many, home is the principal site of freedom and experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware socioeconomic bias in progressive/faddish doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Many modern 'advanced' ideas (e.g., free love, notions of female economic dependence) are rooted in experiences peculiar to the rich and do not generalize to the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging progressive movements or cultural critiques, check whether their assumptions presuppose leisure, servants, or disposable income. Test proposals against the lived conditions of less-privileged groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: True free-thinking judges by the moral 'ought' rather than past/future allegiance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only true free-thinker is he whose intellect is as much free from the future as from the past. He cares only for what ought to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply an abstract independence criterion: evaluate ideas by whether they answer 'what ought to be' rather than aligning uncritically with either nostalgic restoration or utopian futurism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two republican ideals to test revolutionary claims: honorable poverty and extreme publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Revolution presupposed (and temporarily achieved) the ideas of honorable poverty and extreme publicity; these are benchmarks for the fullness of republicanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess modern republican/democratic claims by whether public life preserves austerity/honorable poverty among leaders and genuine publicity/transparency; compare contemporary elites against these historical standards.
